description: INXS's only US No. 1, a late-arriving Kick track built on a riff Andrew Farriss raced back to his motel room to tape, leaving a cab driver waiting 45 minutes.

pops.text: That slinky riff popped into Andrew Farriss's head while he was waiting for a cab to the airport. He told the driver he'd be two minutes — then vanished upstairs to tape it.
The cab meter kept running for about 45 minutes. Farriss came back with a cassette and one very annoyed driver — and INXS's signature song.
In Hong Kong, Michael Hutchence heard the demo and wrote most of the lyrics in about 10 minutes. Within a couple of hours, the pair had a finished track.
This was one of the last songs recorded for Kick, not the planned centrepiece. Producer Chris Thomas heard the Hong Kong demos and knew the album was finally done.
The groove is programmed, not just played: Farriss built it on a Roland TR-707 drum machine, and he says what's on the record is pretty much exactly what he programmed.
On the album it segues straight into 'Mediate.' Engineer David Nicholas synced the two tapes by accident, played them back-to-back, and the join was so perfect he thought something had broken.
Director Richard Lowenstein made the video by cutting up 35mm film and photocopying individual frames, then re-layering them — that's the moving magazine-collage look.
In Britain it flopped first time out, stalling at No. 58 in 1987. Re-released in late 1988, it climbed all the way to No. 2 — INXS's highest UK peak.
It became INXS's only Billboard Hot 100 No. 1, in January 1988, and the combined 'Need You Tonight / Mediate' video won Video of the Year at the 1988 MTV VMAs.

title: Need You Tonight

description: Coldplay's Grammy-winning piano anthem — a late-night Liverpool riff that was filed away for the next album before their manager rescued it for A Rush of Blood to the Head.

pops.text: That looping piano figure came to Chris Martin late one night in a Liverpool studio. He sat down, played it, and knew instantly it was something.
Martin has said the song was inspired by Muse — he admired how they built drama and motion out of repeating piano patterns in alternative rock.
Guitarist Jonny Buckland heard the piano sketch and layered guitar chords over it. Suddenly a solo riff had become a full-band song.
Too late, they thought: the album was basically finished, so the demo was filed under 'Songs for #3' — material meant for the third album.
Their manager Phil Harvey pushed them to rescue it. The band rushed it onto A Rush of Blood to the Head instead — good call.
The video was directed by Dominic Leung and shot at London's ExCeL building in Docklands, with a laser show and a mostly student audience told to stay stoic.
Spot Martin's left hand at the piano: 'maketradefair.com' is scrawled on it, plugging Oxfam's Make Trade Fair campaign. The site itself went defunct in 2004.
Chart-wise it was solid, not huge — No. 9 in the UK and No. 29 on the Billboard Hot 100 — but it spent 15 straight weeks at No. 1 on US Adult Alternative radio.
In 2004 it won Record of the Year at the Grammys. Rolling Stone later placed it at No. 490 on its 500 Greatest Songs of All Time list.

title: Clocks

description: The opening blast of Siamese Dream — Billy Corgan's swipe at the indie scene, built from layered Big Muff fuzz and a drum take recorded until Jimmy Chamberlin's hands bled.

pops.text: This is the opening track and first single from Siamese Dream — but it was one of the last songs Billy Corgan wrote for the album.
Corgan has admitted the opening riff is a straight lift, in his words, from Rush's 'By-Tor and the Snow Dog.' He called Cherub Rock basically the Pumpkins doing Rush at half-time.
The lyric is a jab at the indie world Corgan came from. He said in 1995 it was about his relationship to the indie scene and the media around it.
The band recorded in Marietta, Georgia, partly to get drummer Jimmy Chamberlin away from his Chicago drug contacts. It didn't fully work — he vanished on a multi-day bender during sessions.
Legend from the sessions: Corgan made Chamberlin re-record the Cherub Rock drums over and over until his hands bled — even though, by some accounts, he'd nailed it early.
That guitar wall is the famous Big Muff fuzz, stacked in dense layers. Corgan played most of the guitar and bass himself, with some Siamese Dream tracks running to dozens of overdubs.
Hear the solo swirl? That's tape phasing — the solo recorded to two tapes running slightly out of sync, a favourite Corgan and producer Butch Vig trick.

Director Kevin Kerslake shot the video in one rainy night in a forest on Mount Tamalpais outside San Francisco, entirely on Super 8, then damaged the film on purpose for that broken, dirty look. Corgan hated the shoot — they never worked together again.
It was nominated for Best Hard Rock Performance at the 1994 Grammys, losing to Stone Temple Pilots' 'Plush.' Siamese Dream itself debuted at No. 10 and went four-times platinum.

title: Cherub Rock

description: Dave Grohl's salute to ordinary heroes — demoed alone in his Seattle basement in July 1995 and filmed by Grohl himself as a faceless rescuer running into a burning house.

pops.text: Grohl demoed this alone on an 8-track in his Seattle basement on 17 July 1995 — just a month after the first Foo Fighters album came out.
Bassist Nate Mendel remembers hearing that demo and relaxing: in the Back and Forth documentary he says that's when he knew the band was going to be okay.
No, it's not a secret Kurt Cobain tribute, Grohl insists. On Howard Stern in 1999 he corrected that reading: it's about heroes who are ordinary.
Grohl told VH1 Storytellers he wrote it while watching 1980s movies like Valley Girl, thinking about the everyday people he actually looked up to growing up.
It was the third single from The Colour and the Shape, released 19 January 1998. The album remains the best-selling Foo Fighters record in the US, at over two million copies.
Grohl directed the video himself. A man runs into a burning building to save a baby, then a dog, then a framed photo — and you never see his face.
The baby's and dog's eyes are blacked out on purpose, Grohl explained, so they stand for people in need everywhere, not specific characters.
It looks like one continuous take, but the cuts are hidden in the smoke. It's also the only Foo Fighters video featuring short-lived guitarist Franz Stahl.
On 3 September 2022, at the Wembley tribute to Taylor Hawkins, Hawkins's teenage son Shane played drums on this song — the performance went viral and won him a Drumeo award.

title: My Hero

description: A last-minute, two-week addition to Songs from the Big Chair that became Tears For Fears' defining hit — a sunny 12/8 shuffle carrying a Cold War lyric about power.

pops.text: It started with almost nothing: Roland Orzabal walked in playing two simple, chiming chords on an acoustic guitar, over and over, without thinking much of them.
Producer Chris Hughes heard those two chords and saw a hit. Orzabal was sceptical — he thought the song was too jolly next to the band's darker material.
The original title was 'Everybody Wants To Go To War.' Orzabal hated the line, and he's said when a songwriter dislikes his own lyric, the song dies — so it became 'Rule The World.'
Joe Strummer later claimed that line echoed The Clash's 'Charlie Don't Surf.' Strummer told Musician magazine he confronted Orzabal in a restaurant — and Orzabal handed him a fiver.
It was a last-minute addition, written and recorded in under two weeks at the end of the Big Chair sessions — while 'Shout' had taken weeks just to mix.
That breezy bounce is a 12/8 shuffle on a LinnDrum, a feel Hughes pushed for, inspired by Simple Minds' 'Waterfront' and Linx's 'Throw Away the Key.'
Curt Smith, not Orzabal, sings lead — his relaxed vocal is the sugar on a lyric that's really about power, corruption and Cold War anxiety.
Director Nigel Dick filmed the video in Southern California: Smith drives a vintage Austin-Healey 3000 through the desert, intercut with the band and dancers at a gas station.
It hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on 8 June 1985, won Best British Single at the 1986 Brit Awards, and in 1986 the band re-recorded it as 'Everybody Wants To Run The World' for Sport Aid.

title: Everybody Wants To Rule The World
Hot for Teacher
description: Van Halen's classroom-rock riot from 1984 — Alex's engine-like drum intro, Eddie's tapped fireworks, and an MTV video so rowdy it became Exhibit A in the Senate's 'porn rock' hearings.

pops.text: That revving-engine roar opening the song is no car at all — it's Alex Van Halen layering Simmons electronic pads over acoustic drums in a double-bass shuffle.
The album 1984 was largely recorded at Eddie's own home studio, 5150 — the band working on its own turf, on its own schedule.
Under all the shredding, this is a souped-up blues shuffle. Eddie's solo even flies with no rhythm guitar underneath — just bass and drums holding the floor.
David Lee Roth co-directed the video with Pete Angelus and cast pint-sized lookalikes as kid versions of every band member.
Meet Waldo, the nervous new kid. His squeaky voice belongs to future Saturday Night Live star Phil Hartman, years before fame.
The young Michael Anthony lookalike, Yano Anaya, had just played Grover Dill, the bully's toady, in A Christmas Story.
The teacher strutting across the desks is Norwegian model Lillian Müller — she'd already danced through Rod Stewart's 'Da Ya Think I'm Sexy?' video.
The school is John Marshall High in Los Angeles, the same campus that hosted Grease and Pretty in Pink.
Tipper Gore's PMRC never put this song on its 'Filthy Fifteen' list — but senators still screened this video as Exhibit A at the 1985 'porn rock' hearings.
Chart surprise: for all its MTV fame, the single only peaked at No. 56. It was also the last single and video of Van Halen's original David Lee Roth era.

title: What a Fool Believes
description: The Doobie Brothers' smooth, keyboard-driven No. 1 from Minute by Minute — a Michael McDonald and Kenny Loggins co-write that later became the gold standard of yacht rock.

pops.text: Kenny Loggins hadn't even gotten through Michael McDonald's front door when he heard McDonald noodling this tune at the piano — and already had a hook line ready for it.
Producer Ted Templeman kept nagging McDonald about that piano fragment: finish it, he said, it's a hit. He was right.
The writers bonded over childhood favorites like the Four Seasons' 'Sherry' and 'Walk Like a Man' — and aimed for that same soaring falsetto feel.
Loggins actually released his own version first, on his 1978 album Nightwatch, months before the Doobies' take took off.
Smooth as it sounds, the Doobies struggled to land a take they liked — Templeman himself doubled up on drums to help nail the groove.
The lyric is a quiet heartbreaker: a man meets an old flame and tries to revive a romance that, in truth, never really existed.
Debuting at No. 73, the single climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on April 14, 1979 — one of the few non-disco chart-toppers of that disco-drenched year.
At the 1980 Grammys it pulled off a rare double, winning both Song of the Year and Record of the Year.
A 2005 web series retroactively crowned it the ultimate yacht rock song, awarding it a perfect 100 for 'yacht' — the standard every smooth song since is judged by.
In 2024, the song sailed into the Grammy Hall of Fame, 45 years after it topped the charts.

title: Cult of Personality
description: Living Colour's explosive debut single from Vivid — a riff stumbled onto in a Brooklyn loft, sampled speeches, and a warning about charismatic leaders that never stopped being relevant.

pops.text: That opening voice is Malcolm X, from his 1963 'Message to the Grass Roots' speech — the song starts with history before a note is played.
Vernon Reid stumbled onto that jagged signature riff by accident during a 1987 rehearsal — Corey Glover had sung the notes, and Reid chased them on guitar.
By the end of that single Brooklyn loft rehearsal, the band basically had the whole song. Reid fished the title line from a notebook of ideas he carried everywhere.
Reid's question was a dark one: what makes followers swoon for Gandhi and Mussolini alike? Charisma, he decided, doesn't check morality at the door.
An early draft name-checked Adolf Hitler alongside Stalin and Mussolini. Reid cut Hitler, figuring the point landed without him.
Mick Jagger caught the band at CBGB, produced two demo tracks, and helped land their Epic Records deal — the Stones' own engineer Ed Stasium then produced most of Vivid.
The video cuts between the band and a little girl transfixed by a television — Glover's image of how a cult of personality gets beamed into our heads.
The single hit No. 13 on the Hot 100 and won the Grammy for Best Hard Rock Performance, while Vivid went double platinum.
The video won Best Group Video and Best New Artist at the 1989 MTV Video Music Awards.
Wrestler CM Punk made this his entrance anthem and insisted WWE license it in 2011 — Living Colour even played him to the ring live at WrestleMania 29.

title: Jet
description: Wings' first single from Band on the Run. Note: no contemporary music video was made — this is the official audio (2010 remaster) from Paul McCartney's Topic channel, verified via YouTube oEmbed.

pops.text: Official-audio alert: 'Jet' predates the music-video era, so there is no 1974 promo clip — what you're hearing is the official 2010 remaster.
Paul started writing this one halfway up a mountain in Scotland, near his farm — about as far from a jet plane as songwriting gets.
So who is Jet? For years McCartney said a black Labrador puppy. In his 2021 book The Lyrics, he corrected himself: Jet was Mary's little Shetland pony.
Most of Band on the Run was recorded in Lagos, Nigeria — but 'Jet' was cut entirely back in London at George Martin's AIR Studios.
Paul plays almost everything here himself: vocals, guitar, bass, piano and drums, with Denny Laine and Linda filling out the harmonies.
That punchy saxophone comes from Howie Casey, an old Liverpool mate of Paul's from the pre-Beatles dance-hall days.
Tony Visconti — David Bowie's longtime producer — supplied the orchestration that gives the track its extra lift and drive.
Engineer Geoff Emerick quietly copied the tape to a fresh reel after noticing oxide build-up on the heads — he never told Paul, and credited that save for the song's solid sound.
Released as the album's first single, 'Jet' soared to No. 7 in both the US and the UK in 1974.
Legacy check: Australian rock band Jet literally named themselves after this song.

title: The Power of Love
description: Huey Lewis & The News' first No. 1, written for Back to the Future — Marty McFly's skateboard anthem, complete with Doc Brown crashing the music video in the DeLorean.

pops.text: Director Robert Zemeckis wanted Huey Lewis because his band sounded like Marty McFly's favorite band — quintessentially American, blue-collar rock.
Lewis balked: he didn't write movie songs, and he refused to write one called 'Back to the Future.' Zemeckis shrugged: just write whatever you want.
So Lewis, guitarist Chris Hayes and sax man Johnny Colla handed in the very next song they wrote — and never mentioned time travel in it once.
In the film, this is Marty's skateboard dash to school — he hitches rides on bumpers while the chorus begs, 'Don't need money, don't take fame.'
Best inside joke in the movie: the horn-rimmed judge who tells Marty's band they're 'just too darn loud' is Huey Lewis himself, uncredited — rejecting his own song.
Watch the video's club crowd: Doc Brown himself, Christopher Lloyd, pulls up outside in the DeLorean, checks the scene, and drives off.
The video was shot at Uncle Charlie's, a real club the band had played in their scuffling early days — a hometown room for a suddenly huge band.
The single debuted at a modest No. 46 — then the film opened, and by August 24, 1985 it was the band's first No. 1, holding for two weeks.
It was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Song, losing to Lionel Richie's 'Say You, Say Me' — and also earned a Grammy nod for Record of the Year.
The band gave the film a second song too, 'Back in Time,' which plays over the end credits — making Huey Lewis the unofficial sound of 1985 Hill Valley.

title: Back on the Chain Gang
description: Pretenders' biggest U.S. hit, written by Chrissie Hynde as a memorial to guitarist James Honeyman-Scott and recorded by a band down to two members. Official music video from the Pretenders channel.

pops.text: Chrissie Hynde started this song about her relationship with Ray Davies of The Kinks — then tragedy rewrote it completely.
Recording began on July 20, 1982, at AIR Studios in London — barely a month after the band fell apart.
Guitarist James Honeyman-Scott had died at 25, just two days after bassist Pete Farndon was fired. Only Hynde and drummer Martin Chambers were left.
Hynde cut the vocal while about three months pregnant with her first daughter, whose father was Ray Davies.
Stand-ins saved the session: Rockpile's Billy Bremner played that lyrical lead guitar, Big Country's Tony Butler played bass, and Robbie McIntosh joined in.
Hear that hammer clang? A studio tech banged together two 25-pound weights used to steady microphone booms — in time, by hand, no sampler.
Those 'ooh-aah' backing vocals are a deliberate tip of the hat to Sam Cooke's 1960 soul classic 'Chain Gang.'
The video tells the story by itself: it features only Hynde and Chambers, because they were the only two Pretenders left.
The B-side, 'My City Was Gone,' became a hit in its own right — Hynde's lament for her changed Ohio hometown.
It peaked at No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 — still the Pretenders' biggest hit in America. Hynde dedicated it to Honeyman-Scott.

title: Dance Hall Days
description: Wang Chung's nostalgic new-wave hit — first released under their original name Huang Chung, then re-recorded at Abbey Road for Points on the Curve. Official VEVO video (the Derek Jarman version).

pops.text: This song had two lives: first released in October 1982 when the band was still called Huang Chung, it flopped — so they re-recorded it.
That name, Huang Chung — later Wang Chung — translates from Mandarin as 'yellow bell.'
Jack Hues wrote it from real memory: his dad played in an old-fashioned dance hall band, and young Jack used to play in that band too.
Hues says the lyric starts innocent — 'take your baby by the hand' — and gets hallucinogenic by the last verse, amethyst and all.
The groove is sneakily tricky: a shuffly three-against-two feel, partly inspired by an Adam and the Ants track.
Nick Feldman later recalled the song even reached Quincy Jones while Jones was producing Michael Jackson's Thriller — Wang Chung kept it for themselves.
Two videos were made. This first one, by Derek Jarman, uses his father's early colour home movies — the toddler in the footage is Jarman himself.
Spot the ending here: the band dress as Wizard of Oz characters — Hues as the Tin Man, Nick Feldman as the Scarecrow, Darren Costin as the Cowardly Lion.
A second, 1940s fantasy video got heavy MTV rotation and a Best New Artist nomination at the first MTV VMAs in 1984, losing to Eurythmics' 'Sweet Dreams.'

It hit No. 16 in the U.S., No. 1 on Billboard's dance chart, and No. 21 at home — Wang Chung's only UK Top 40 single. Director William Friedkin loved it so much he hired the band to score To Live and Die in L.A.

title: Viva La Vida
description: Coldplay's fallen-king anthem and first No. 1 in both the U.S. and UK, from Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends. Official Hype Williams video, with the band performing inside Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People.

pops.text: 'Viva la vida' is Spanish for 'long live life' — Chris Martin borrowed the phrase from a painting by Mexican artist Frida Kahlo.
The artwork behind the band is Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People — the same painting used for the album cover.
Producer Brian Eno set a rule for the album sessions: every single song had to sound different from the others.
This was Coldplay's first album produced by Eno, and the band used the sessions to deliberately break their own formula.
Coldplay first performed the song live at the 2008 MTV Movie Awards, just before the album came out.
Director Hype Williams premiered this video on Coldplay's website on August 1, 2008 — watch the band crumble into rose petals at the end.
There's a second official video: Anton Corbijn filmed Martin in The Hague as a wandering king, a tribute to Corbijn's own 'Enjoy the Silence' video for Depeche Mode.
It became Coldplay's first No. 1 single in both the U.S. and UK — the first British act to top both charts at once in the 21st century.
At the 2009 Grammys it won Song of the Year and Best Pop Performance by a Duo or Group, while the album won Best Rock Album.
Guitarist Joe Satriani sued, claiming it borrowed from his 2004 instrumental 'If I Could Fly.' Coldplay denied it, and the case was dismissed in September 2009 after the sides settled.

title: Werewolves of London
description: Warren Zevon's only Top 40 hit — a 15-minute joke song that became his signature. Official Rhino music video; Zevon's longtime collaborator Jorge Calderón plays the werewolf in the promotional clip (per warrenzevon.com).

pops.text: This began as a joke: Phil Everly of the Everly Brothers saw the 1935 film Werewolf of London on TV and dared Zevon to make it a dance song.
Zevon, LeRoy Marinell and Waddy Wachtel wrote it in about 15 minutes at Marinell's Venice home — Zevon's wife Crystal wrote down the lyrics as they shouted them.
Nobody took it seriously. Zevon called it 'a dumb song for smart people' and didn't want it as a single — the label insisted.
Jackson Browne believed in it early: he produced Excitable Boy and had been playing 'Werewolves' in his own concerts since about 1975.
That's a famous rhythm section: Fleetwood Mac's Mick Fleetwood on drums and John McVie on bass, with Zevon on piano.
After years of failed attempts dating back to 1974, they finally captured the magic on just the second take.
In the promotional video, the werewolf is played by Jorge Calderón — Zevon's friend and frequent co-writer.
Lee Ho Fook's was real: a Chinatown restaurant on Gerrard Street in Soho, where a hungry werewolf could indeed get beef chow mein.
It peaked at No. 21 — Zevon's only Top 40 hit — and helped push Excitable Boy to No. 8 and platinum.
Thirty years later, Kid Rock built 'All Summer Long' on this song's piano groove, mashed up with 'Sweet Home Alabama' — and Zevon's writers got credited.

title: In the Meantime
description: Spacehog's glammy debut single from Resident Alien — English expats in New York channelling Bowie and Queen. Official music video via Rhino.

pops.text: That ringing, dial-tone intro isn't a phone at all — it's a sample of the Penguin Cafe Orchestra's 'Telephone and Rubber Band.'
Resident aliens indeed: Spacehog were Englishmen from West Yorkshire who formed the band after moving to New York City in 1994.
Brothers Royston and Antony Langdon started out singing in the Leeds Parish Church Choir as kids — a long way from glam rock.
Most of debut album Resident Alien was recorded live in a barn in Woodstock, New York, to capture a real room sound.
Drummer Jonny Cragg suggested flying in backwards piano chords like Queen's 'Another One Bites the Dust' — and the outro drums deliberately nod to 'We Will Rock You.'
Cragg recalled that Sean Lennon visited the session, and Royston ended up cutting the single on a Rickenbacker bass borrowed from John Lennon's collection.
Royston Langdon said in 2018 the song is about a search for the end of isolation — and learning to accept yourself.
It topped Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart for four weeks and the UK Rock chart, reaching No. 32 on the Hot 100 and No. 29 in the UK.
Resident Alien went gold, selling 500,000 copies in its first eight months, largely on this single's MTV and radio play.
It refuses to die: re-recorded for Guitar Hero 5, the original in Rock Band 3, and back on screen in Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3.
